edges.description: Deep neck spread from the oropharyngeal focus seeds the lateral pharyngeal and carotid-sheath region, where the hallmark internal-jugular septic thrombus forms.
The oropharyngeal F. necrophorum population elaborates leukotoxin and other virulence factors that mediate immune evasion.
Acute pharyngotonsillar infection produces the antecedent sore throat.

Leukotoxin-mediated immune evasion is thought to permit the anaerobic invasion that seeds the internal-jugular septic thrombus. The human thrombus-initiation step is inferred from bovine leukotoxin experiments rather than directly demonstrated.
Fragments and bacteria from the infected jugular thrombus embolize hematogenously, most often to the lungs.
Emboli lodging in the pulmonary vasculature produce septic pulmonary emboli, the dominant metastatic complication.
Pulmonary septic emboli can produce hemoptysis.
Bacteremia and metastatic emboli progress to systemic sepsis and its complications.
Systemic infection manifests as sepsis in most patients.
Systemic invasive infection produces thrombocytopenia on admission.
A subset of septic patients progress to septic shock.
Systemic infection produces the near-universal fever.

nodes.description: Fever is the most common presenting feature of pediatric Lemierre syndrome, reported in 92% of cases in a systematic review.

evidence.reference_title: Pediatric Lemierre's syndrome: A systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Fever was the most common presenting symptom in 92% of patients, and F. necrophorum was the predominantly identified organism in 78.3% of patients.

nodes.description: F. necrophorum virulence is dominated by leukotoxin, with endotoxin and other secreted products also implicated. Bovine leukocyte experiments show that purified leukotoxin activates polymorphonuclear leukocytes at low concentrations, induces apoptotic/programmed death at higher concentrations, and produces necrotic death at very high concentrations; this mechanism is strong model support for immune evasion but the human internal-jugular thrombus-initiation step remains inferred.

evidence.reference_title: Fusobacterium necrophorum infections: virulence factors, pathogenic mechanism and control measures.
evidence.snippet: Among these, leukotoxin and endotoxin are believed to be more important than other toxins in overcoming the host's defence mechanisms to establish the infection.

evidence.reference_title: Fusobacterium necrophorum leukotoxin induces activation and apoptosis of bovine leukocytes.
evidence.snippet: The ability of F. necrophorum leukotoxin to modulate the host immune system by its toxicity, including cellular activation of PMNs and apoptosis-mediated killing of phagocytes and immune effector cells, represents a potentially important mechanism of its pathogenesis.

nodes.description: Pulmonary septic emboli can produce hemoptysis as part of the lower respiratory presentation.

evidence.reference_title: [Lemierre syndrome: several clinical features of "a forgotten disease"].
evidence.snippet: One of the 6 developed acute renal failure, another one hemoptysis, and another a hydropneumothorax which was drained.

nodes.description: Infection reaching the deep neck spaces triggers a septic thrombus in the internal jugular vein. F. necrophorum hemagglutinin, hemolysin, proteases, adhesin, and endothelial injury are plausible contributors to coagulation, but direct human proof of platelet-driven thrombus initiation is limited.

evidence.reference_title: Early Radiographic Warning Signs of Impending Lemierre's Syndrome.
evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of Lemierre's syndrome is typically confirmed through the identification of thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein on radiographic imaging and the isolation of anaerobic bacteria in blood cultures.

evidence.reference_title: Fusobacterium necrophorum infections in animals: pathogenesis and pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence.snippet: Several toxins or secreted products, such as leukotoxin, endotoxin, hemolysin, hemagglutinin, proteases, and adhesin, etc., have been implicated as virulence factors.

nodes.description: Acute pharyngotonsillar infection is the usual initiating focus. F. necrophorum, and less often odontogenic streptococci or other anaerobes, invade from the upper aerodigestive tract into adjacent deep neck spaces.

evidence.reference_title: Early diagnosis of Lemierre syndrome using targeted next-generation sequencing combined with metagenomics capture: A case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: Lemierre syndrome (LS) is a rare but life-threatening complication of acute oropharyngeal infections.

evidence.reference_title: Excision of the internal jugular vein in uncontrolled Lemierre's syndrome: a case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: Although the classic form is usually associated with oropharyngeal infection and Fusobacterium necrophorum, odontogenic and non-Fusobacterium cases have also been reported.

nodes.description: Empiric and targeted treatment uses prolonged broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy that covers anaerobes, commonly a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor or a third-generation cephalosporin combined with metronidazole; carbapenems are an alternative broad-spectrum regimen.

evidence.reference_title: Lemierre's syndrome secondary to fusobacterium necrophorum in an immunocompetent patient: A rare case.
evidence.snippet: Immediate treatment involves broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, often utilizing a third-generation cephalosporin or a beta-lactam in combination with metronidazole.

evidence.reference_title: [Lemierre syndrome: several clinical features of "a forgotten disease"].
evidence.snippet: All the patients were managed with antibiotics against anaerobes, carbapenems in 3 cases.

nodes.description: Septic emboli seeded from the internal jugular thrombus disseminate to the lungs, producing the typical respiratory branch of Lemierre syndrome with septic pulmonary emboli, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, and severe pleural or parenchymal complications in some patients.

evidence.reference_title: [Lemierre syndrome: several clinical features of "a forgotten disease"].
evidence.snippet: RESULTS: We had 6 patients with LS. 5 males. Median age: 25 years old. All with sore throat and pulmonary embolisms.

evidence.reference_title: Pediatric Lemierre's syndrome: A systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Computed tomography (CT) imaging was utilized in 89.5% of cases, and was most useful for detecting thrombosis of the internal jugular vein and septic emboli.

nodes.description: Anticoagulation is considered only as an adjunct for selected thrombus patterns or high-risk cases because its indications in Lemierre syndrome remain controversial.

evidence.reference_title: Anticoagulation Strategies in the Management of Lemierre Syndrome: A Systematic Review of the Literature.
evidence.snippet: Anticoagulation in LS is a clinical controversy because the thromboembolic events have rarely led to significant complications; thrombi typically resolve independently, and concerns for bleeding risks are well founded; however, this review indicates both the efficacy and safety of anticoagulation.

nodes.description: Internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis and metastatic embolization commonly progress to sepsis.

evidence.reference_title: Invasive infections with Fusobacterium necrophorum including Lemierre's syndrome: an 8-year Swedish nationwide retrospective study.
evidence.snippet: Among patients with LS 72/96 (75%) had thrombocytopenia on admission, 86/104 (83%) had sepsis, 19/104 (18%) developed septic shock and 45/104 (43%) needed intensive care.

nodes.description: Septic pulmonary emboli are the dominant metastatic complication after internal jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis.

evidence.reference_title: Lemierre's syndrome secondary to fusobacterium necrophorum in an immunocompetent patient: A rare case.
evidence.snippet: Lemierre syndrome is a rare and life-threatening condition that typically arises secondary to an oropharyngeal infection, progressing to thrombosis of the internal jugular vein and dissemination of septic emboli, most commonly to the lungs.

nodes.description: A subset of patients progress from sepsis to septic shock and intensive-care-level illness.
